decision.state: No demonstrated all-cause readmission benefit; exploratory heart-failure model only
decision.summary: Project Open Hand directly delivered meals in two randomized trials, which is unusually relevant organization evidence for a local charity. The largest trial found no improvement in its primary all-cause hospitalization outcome. A favorable heart-failure hospitalization result was exploratory, provider-pooled, and not a Project Open Hand estimate. Market for Impact therefore models that narrower hypothesis separately rather than calling the whole organization cost-effective.
decision.costEffectiveness: Primary endpoint: no demonstrated benefit. Exploratory heart-failure hypothesis: approximately $212,500 per additional 90-day heart-failure hospitalization averted; $56,604-$1.4 million conditional positive-effect sensitivity; null effect plausible
decision.roomForMoreFunding: Not published for the modeled pathway

financialContext.summary: The FY2024 audit reports $13.47 million in total assets and $6.91 million available for general expenditure within one year.
financialContext.boundary: Audited organization-wide amounts are capacity and liquidity context. They are not the cost of the medically tailored meal intervention, unrestricted surplus, or room for more funding.

evidence.population: 1,977 recently hospitalized high-risk adults in Northern California; Project Open Hand and Ceres delivered meals
evidence.result: The primary all-cause 90-day hospitalization outcome was not improved: 27.1% with meals versus 24.6% with usual care, a 2.6-point adverse risk difference (95% CI -1.3 to 6.5) and adjusted hazard ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.86-1.21). Among 641 participants with heart failure, an exploratory analysis found 7.9% versus 13.2% heart-failure hospitalization, a -5.3-point difference (95% CI -10.0 to -0.6) and adjusted hazard ratio 0.52 (95% CI 0.32-0.86).
evidence.transfer: This is the strongest evidence and directly involved Project Open Hand, but it combines two providers and five medical centers. The heart-failure result was exploratory and must not replace the null primary result. Our model discounts the 5.3-point subgroup difference and keeps a null effect plausible.

evidence.population: 191 Project Open Hand clients living with HIV; intensive food-plus-nutrition support versus less-intensive Project Open Hand standard care
evidence.result: At six months, the intensive arm had lower odds of hospitalization, food insecurity, depressive symptoms, poor antiretroviral adherence, and unprotected sex. The trial found no difference in its primary viral-nonsuppression or health-related-quality-of-life outcomes.
evidence.transfer: This is organization-specific and locally relevant, but small, population-specific, and a comparison of two Project Open Hand service intensities rather than food support versus no service. It does not identify the heart-failure effect or cost used in our model.

evidence.population: Medi-Cal beneficiaries with congestive heart failure across eight California counties; Project Open Hand served San Francisco, Alameda, and San Mateo
evidence.result: The authorizing program set a $6 million four-year budget to serve 1,413 beneficiaries with three medically tailored meals per day for 12 weeks. That implies $4,246 per targeted participant before any distinction between budget, contracted price, actual spending, provider cost, or current price. The final evaluation pooled multiple providers and did not publish a Project Open Hand-only causal estimate.
evidence.transfer: We round the public program budget ratio to a $4,250 best-guess course cost and use a wide $3,000-$7,000 range. It is the closest program-specific public anchor, but the intensity differs from the randomized trial's one large meal per day for up to 10 weeks and is not current philanthropic funding room.

model.nativeOutcome: An additional 90-day hospitalization for heart failure averted among a recently discharged adult with known heart failure because a medically tailored meal course was offered
missingInputs: A named current Project Open Hand post-discharge heart-failure program, legal entity, service geography, eligibility rule, and meal intensity for the proposed gift
Project Open Hand-only eligible, enrolled, reached, completing, and followed participant counts with reasons for nonparticipation and missingness
Current incremental food, delivery, dietitian, referral, data, and shared costs per completed course, separated from reimbursed services
Pre-specified Project Open Hand-only all-cause and heart-failure hospitalization outcomes with a credible comparison and 90-day follow-up
Payer reimbursement, public-program coverage, private-gift displacement, and the counterfactual for eligible patients not philanthropically funded
A time-bounded $100K, $1M, and $10M capacity plan with incremental courses, constraints, milestones, downside cases, and stop rules
model.qalyBoundary: No QALY, WELLBY, life-saved, or life-substantially-bettered conversion is published. First confirm a targeted Project Open Hand hospitalization effect; then model duration, mortality overlap, quality of life, and hospitalization disutility separately.

reservations: The largest randomized trial missed its primary all-cause hospitalization outcome; the favorable heart-failure result was exploratory.
The heart-failure subgroup result combined Project Open Hand and Ceres and does not identify a provider-specific effect.

The randomized intervention delivered one large meal per day for up to 10 weeks, while the state pilot cost anchor covered three meals per day for 12 weeks plus nutrition and case-management components.
Only 53.5% of randomized meal recipients received all 10 weeks, and those receiving more than five weeks differed from those receiving fewer.
The smaller HIV trial found no effect on its primary viral or health-related-quality-of-life outcomes and compared intensive with standard Project Open Hand service.
FY2024 scale combines several programs and three counties, so dividing organization expenses by meals or clients would be misleading.
Public financing, health-plan reimbursement, and philanthropy may all support medically tailored nutrition; the current private-gift counterfactual is not published.
No current organization-supplied marginal plan for a post-discharge heart-failure cohort was found in the reviewed public sources.
